The Poisson Autoregressive model has been widely used to forecast count-based
time series data. However, its fixed parameter assumption limits its ability
to adapt to changing data patterns. In contrast, the non-parametric nature of
Kernel Ridge Regression allows for temporal variations in the data, but at the
cost of forgoing sparsity and interpretability. To address this trade-off, we
propose a novel approach called Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregression (TVPA)
that combines the strengths of both models. TVPA employs a time-varying kernel
to capture changes in the data, while utilizing a sparse and interpretable
Poisson Autoregressive model as a prior. To adapt to changing patterns, TVPA
employs a dynamic kernel that is learned through a change-point detection
algorithm. We demonstrate the efficacy of TVPA in adapting to changes in data
via extensive experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our
results show that TVPA outperforms static models and offers comparable
performance to non-parametric baselines while providing a sparse and interpretable
model. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical guarantee for TVPA's convergence
rate under mild conditions. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/kuanghou/TVPA.

This approach results in a pose-invariant, compact, and action-relevant representation of objects, which we term "action descriptors." To train NDFs, we developed a neural network that can be trained using a combination of neural descriptor loss and a neural network-based occupancy loss. This network is capable of generating action descriptors from raw sensor data and estimating the future pose of objects in manipulation tasks. We demonstrated the effectiveness of NDFs in a robotic manipulation task using a simulated environment and a real-world setup with a robotic arm. Pose estimation with six degrees of freedom (DoF) is a challenging task, particularly when objects have complex shapes and multiple views. Deep learning-based approaches have shown significant improvements in pose estimation, but they often struggle with objects that have intricate shapes and multiple views. To address these challenges, we propose a novel pose estimation framework called DeepHMap++, which integrates projection grouping and correspondence learning to accurately determine the 6-DoF pose of objects with complex shapes and multiple views. In projection grouping, a novel projection grouping module is introduced to divide the object into distinct regions based on its 3D geometry, which enables the network to focus on specific regions and reduce the impact of occlusions and background interference. To establish correspondences between the 2D image and 3D model, a correspondence learning module is proposed that uses a novel correspondence loss function to directly predict the correspondences between the 2D image and 3D model. To evaluate our approach, we conducted experiments on the BOP and LMO datasets, and the results show that DeepHMap++ achieves superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods. The accuracy of medical image analysis is heavily reliant on high-quality input data, and MRI images are no exception. However, technical issues during image acquisition can lead to artifacts, causing problems for deep learning models. Despite this challenge, little research has been conducted on detecting image acquisition problems using deep learning. In this study, we trained a deep learning model to identify various MRI quality issues simultaneously, using a large dataset of 3D brain MRI images. The model was able to detect 15 different types of problems, including artifacts caused by motion, metal objects, and other technical issues. By analyzing the model's performance, we found that it could accurately identify most problems, but struggled with certain similar issues, such as distinguishing between different types of cardiac artifacts. To address this limitation, we modified the model to focus on the most common problems, and it was able to achieve high levels of accuracy on unseen data, even when new problems were introduced. This success has implications for using deep learning models to evaluate the quality of MRI images, and highlights the importance of considering technical issues during image acquisition. To facilitate further research, we have made the model and dataset available online. The significance of context in object recognition has been extensively debated.
While some argue that context plays a vital role, others claim it is inconsequential.
This paper delves into the underlying reasons behind this discrepancy by examining the
various approaches used to assess the impact of context in the deep learning era.
We analyze the methods employed to evaluate the influence of context and highlight
the limitations of each, which contribute to the ambiguity surrounding this issue.
We also propose a novel context assessment framework that considers both the
object's local and global context, leveraging a combination of spatial attention and
top-down guidance.
This framework enables the extraction of both intrinsic and extrinsic context
features, which are then integrated to facilitate accurate object classification.
We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on the PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012
datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance and providing valuable insights into
the context assessment process. We believe this work provides a clear and concise
method for evaluating the influence of context in deep object recognition networks.

Reinforcement learning agents can excel at optimizing complex policies, but they often struggle to adapt to new situations outside their training environment. To overcome this limitation, agents are often trained on a diverse set of experiences, known as a replay buffer, to improve their policy's robustness and performance. However, the existing experience replay methods suffer from a significant issue: they prioritize the most confident data points, which are often the easiest cases, over the most uncertain ones. This can lead to agents becoming overly confident in their abilities and failing to generalize effectively. To address this challenge, we propose a novel experience replay method called Variance Decrease based Experience Replay (VDER), which selects the most uncertain data points to prioritize over the most confident ones. VDER uses a simple yet effective variance-based criterion to identify the most uncertain data points and incorporates a temperature parameter to balance the exploration-exploitation trade-off. We demonstrate the efficacy of VDER in enhancing the performance of agents in challenging situations, both in simulated and real-world environments, by training them on diverse experiences and transferring the policies to new situations. We also provide a theoretical analysis of VDER's convergence properties and show that it maintains the same convergence rate as the original experience replay method. We make our code publicly available for further research.

When engaging in conversations, people often use different sentence meanings to
elicit the same response from their conversation partners. This phenomenon is
evident in various linguistic constructions, such as questions with different
forms, and even in the same question form, as seen in the example: "Who did
you see?" and "Did you see who?". This semantic variety in conversations can
be viewed as a form of natural language inference, where the intended meaning of
one sentence is inferred from another. We propose a new task called Inference
Variety in Conversations (IVC), which involves selecting the most suitable
inference relation from a set of options to represent the variety of sentence
meanings used in a given conversation. We also introduce a dataset called
Conversational Natural Language Inference (ConveNLI) to facilitate the
development of IVC. Our findings suggest that IVC is a challenging task that
requires a deeper understanding of the underlying semantics of the conversation
and the NLI relations. We propose a straightforward approach that leverages
pre-trained language models to represent the conversation's semantic structure
and employs a graph attention network to select the most suitable NLI relation.

natural language generation and question answering. Our work provides a starting

to enhance our understanding of the underlying semantics of conversations. We

Researchers have extensively studied random walks on various lattices, yet the underlying dynamics of these processes remain poorly understood when the systems exhibit critical behavior. In this study, we analyze a simple random walk on a Cayley tree within the critical regime of a specific class of quenched random potentials. By employing an independent identification of the system's disorder operator in relation to the potential's average value, we derive an algebraic expression for the distribution of the system's state at the scale of avalanches. This expression is characterized by a single parameter that reflects the interplay between the system's critical temperature and the dispersion of the random potential. We further demonstrate that this parameter remains unaffected by the system's size, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of the distribution's asymptotic behavior. Additionally, we compare our findings to those obtained from the droplet theory, and we discuss the implications of our results for the dynamics of the Ising model in its disordered and random-field versions. We also examine the connection to the Bethe lattice and the effects of bond randomness on the system's behavior. Finally, we outline the possibilities for future research and the potential applications of our findings to other related models.

However, the current paradigm is challenged by the emergence of new classes in tasks with a massive number of predefined classes, such as ImageNet. Traditional methods that rely on pre-trained models with a fixed number of classes face difficulties when encountering unknown classes. In contrast, end-to-end deep learning methods can adapt to new classes but are hindered by the requirement for a massive amount of data to be effective. By introducing a class-activation based dynamic graph neural network, our method is able to selectively focus on a subset of samples that are relevant to the new classes, thereby achieving superior performance with a significantly reduced number of data. Furthermore, we extend our method to tackle the multi-label classification problem on ImageNet, achieving a new state-of-the-art performance of 83.4% top-1 accuracy on a 1 million-class dataset with only 1000 classes. In recent years, neural networks have been used to generate synthetic gradients for accelerated asynchronous distributed training. This method has been shown to be effective in reducing communication costs and accelerating convergence speed. However, generating high-quality synthetic gradients requires solving a non-convex optimization problem for each parameter update, which is computationally expensive and difficult to implement. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a neural network to directly acquire gradients without the need for optimization. Specifically, we train a Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN) to represent the gradient field using a Hamiltonian dynamics system, and then use the Hamiltonian dynamics system to generate gradients by solving a differential equation. We demonstrate that this approach yields high-quality synthetic gradients that match the performance of the original baselines in various scenarios, including convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and large language models. Moreover, our method significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art in terms of FLOPs reduction ratio. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method, showing that the HNN network can be viewed as a non-linear transformation that preserves the norm of the gradients. To facilitate further research, we have made our code publicly available on GitHub. We also discuss the limitations of our approach and potential avenues for future improvement.

Furthermore, the increasing reliance on automated data collection methods has led to a rise in biased and incomplete datasets. In response to these challenges, we propose a novel multi-agent approach that incorporates human feedback to assess the trustworthiness of machine learning models. This system, which we call TRUST, utilizes a rating system to evaluate the reliability of the models and incorporates human input to amplify the most critical data points. This results in a more robust and dependable machine learning model that can handle complex, dynamic environments. We have tested TRUST on a range of scenarios, including those with varying levels of uncertainty, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Word Sense Discrimination (WSD) is a critical task within Natural Language Processing, 
aiming to accurately identify the intended sense of a word in context. 
Traditionally, WSD models rely on pre-trained language models to capture contextual 
information, but often overlook the value of gloss information associated with each 
word sense. In this study, we explore the role of gloss information in enhancing WSD 
performance. Specifically, we investigate the impact of incorporating gloss information 
into the input of a BERT-based model through a technique called Context-Gloss 
Augmentation. Our findings reveal that this method significantly boosts WSD performance 
across multiple datasets. Furthermore, we analyze the effects of varying the method's 
parameters and discover that Context-Gloss Augmentation is particularly effective when 
the word senses are highly semantically distinct. To streamline the process, we also 
introduce a technique called Context-Gloss Embedding, which leverages the inherent 
semantic properties of gloss information to enhance the model's input. Our results 
demonstrate that this method yields superior outcomes when compared to traditional WSD 
approaches. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the pivotal role of gloss 
information in WSD and provides actionable guidelines for incorporating it effectively 
into the BERT-based model. Our proposed methods are made available for public use.

However, reconstructing accurate surface models from limited CT data is challenging due to its two-dimensional nature. Researchers have explored the use of volume-to-surface registration techniques to enhance surface models, yet these methods often prioritize alignment over biomechanical accuracy. To address this limitation, a novel approach is proposed that combines a data-driven biomechanical model with a non-rigid volume-to-surface alignment technique. The proposed method leverages a reduced-order model to simulate surface deformation and a novel optimization framework that balances alignment and biomechanical fidelity. The approach is demonstrated using a dataset of 20 porcine lungs, and the results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional techniques in terms of biomechanical similarity and surface deformation accuracy. Furthermore, the method's efficiency is highlighted by the ability to handle large datasets and the use of a compact reduced-order model. The proposed technique has the potential to enhance the realism of lung simulation training and can be applied to other organs with complex geometries. Estimating scene flow from a single image is a challenging task due to the lack of a second image as a reference. To address this issue, researchers have explored the application of metric learning in monocular scene flow estimation, where the goal is to establish a correspondence between the depth map and a reconstructed 3D point cloud using a learned metric. However, existing methods rely heavily on the accuracy of the reconstructed 3D point cloud, which can be compromised by the quality of the input data. In contrast, we propose a novel approach called Adversarial Metric Learning for Self-Guided Scene Flow Estimation, which bypasses the use of a reconstructed 3D point cloud and directly learns a correspondence between the depth map and its neighborhood. The learned metric is then used to guide the scene flow estimation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through comprehensive experiments on several datasets, including the KITTI dataset, and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The code for this work is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yang/Adversarial-Scene-Flow-Estimation.

Modern cloud-native applications comprise numerous microservices running within containers, leading to a surge in system calls from containers. This growth poses a significant threat to the security of these systems. Current solutions either rely on system call monitoring across all containers or employ static policy configurations, which are either overly permissive or fail to account for changing service requirements. In contrast, our research introduces Timeloops, a novel approach that autonomously learns container system call policies based on observed behavior. This approach leverages a combination of machine learning algorithms and system call metadata to create a policy that can be applied to past, present, and future system call patterns. Our evaluation demonstrates a 2.5x reduction in allowed system calls compared to a baseline policy, while maintaining a 99% accuracy in predicting system calls for a real-world containerized application. Furthermore, Timeloops can be easily integrated into existing container runtime environments with minimal overhead. Our research provides a foundation for a more dynamic and adaptive approach to managing container system calls in cloud-native applications.

Coreference resolution is a crucial component in NLP tasks, enabling the identification of entities that refer to the same thing within a text. Despite advancements in this area, research has shown that state-of-the-art models often struggle with centering, a key principle that governs how speakers link successive utterances. This study delves into the relationship between centering and coreference resolution, examining whether a strong connection exists. Through the use of centering theory, we developed a novel evaluation metric to assess the ability of models to adhere to this principle. By applying this metric to multiple datasets, we discovered that there is no direct correlation between a model's adherence to centering theory and its performance in coreference resolution. Furthermore, we found that centering theory does not provide a significant improvement over existing baselines in coreference resolution tasks. These findings suggest that the connection between centering and coreference resolution is more complex than previously thought and that future research should focus on developing more nuanced methods to evaluate the relationship between these two concepts.

Researchers often collect data from social networks to study peer effects, but estimating the influence of network peers on individual outcomes is challenging due to endogeneity. A recent study proposes a method to estimate peer effects using network data, but it assumes a fully linear regression model, which may not be suitable for many real-world scenarios. In contrast, we investigate a partially linear regression model, where the relationship between the outcome and a set of covariates is linear, but the connection between the outcome and the network variables is nonlinear. Under certain conditions, we derive the asymptotic distribution of the plug-in estimator for the non-linear parameter and provide a simulation study to demonstrate its performance. Furthermore, we apply this method to estimate the non-linear peer influence in a network data set, where the effect of network peers on an individual's smoking behavior is analyzed using the Adderall Health and Recovery Network. The results show that the estimated non-linear peer influence varies across different levels of the covariates and the network measures, and it is stronger for individuals with lower levels of education. Additionally, we propose a test for the non-linearity of peer effects and reject the null hypothesis of linearity in this data set. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the design of interventions targeting smoking behavior. The supplementary materials include the R code for the simulation study and the network data set. Proteins can form intricate knots within their three-dimensional structures, and these knots can resist unwinding under mechanical stress. Recent studies suggest that the paths these proteins take during folding are influenced by topological constraints, potentially favoring specific knot-bending pathways over others. However, pinpointing these pathways in knotted proteins proves to be a challenging task. We developed a statistical approach to identify preferred knot-bending pathways based on the three-dimensional structures of knotted proteins. This method was applied to proteins knotted in the shape of trefoil knots, allowing us to compare the predicted pathways with actual structures and determine that there are distinct preferred pathways. These pathways are influenced by the proteins' chemical properties and can be used to guide simulations of protein folding. Furthermore, we found that proteins with trefoil knots tend to favor pathways that involve the crossing 4$_{1}$-shift, a previously undiscovered pattern of movement. This shift is distinct from other known patterns and could be an essential feature of protein folding under topological constraints. This finding is supported by simulations of protein folding using a coarse-grained model. We also found that proteins with trefoil knots that have a knot that is more deeply embedded tend to favor pathways that involve the 4$_{1}$-shift more frequently than proteins with a less embedded knot. This discovery is significant because it provides a possible explanation for why some proteins with trefoil knots are more resistant to unwinding than others. This study demonstrates the importance of considering topological constraints when studying protein folding and the potential for cross-over between chemistry and topology in the folding of proteins with knots. This research also highlights the potential of statistical analysis of protein structures to reveal patterns of protein folding that are influenced by chemistry and topology. This study focused on proteins with trefoil knots, but the methods developed here can be applied to proteins with other types of knots. In this talk, we delve into the specifics of a Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem that deviates from its standard form, focusing on its peculiar characteristics. A particular class of symmetry breakings, where the shift in the symmetry and the resulting long-range force have opposite signs, serve as prime examples of this unusual phenomenon. We examine the conditions under which such unusual NG scenarios emerge, exploring both relativistic and non-relativistic contexts. The unique characteristics of graphene serve as an ideal substrate for the epitaxial growth of thin films, allowing researchers to explore novel phenomena such as remote epitaxy. In this study, we investigated the epitaxial growth of a Heusler alloy, Co2MnSi, on a graphene/sapphire substrate and observed a transition from van der Waals to remote epitaxy. By analyzing the structural and chemical properties of the grown films, we found that the remote epitaxy equilibrium can be influenced by both lattice mismatch and surface chemistry, and that a critical mismatch threshold of 4.5% is necessary to achieve remote epitaxy. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the remote epitaxy equilibrium can be shifted by introducing a lattice-matched Heusler alloy, Fe3GeTe2, through co-deposition, allowing for the control of epitaxial growth modes. These findings provide a foundation for the controlled growth of thin films on graphene substrates and highlight the potential of Heusler alloys as a model system for exploring the unique properties of remote epitaxy.

The upper bound represents the solution to a classical problem of minimizing expected time until exit from a domain defined by two moving boundaries, and the lower bound is associated with a problem of the same type but with reversed boundary dynamics. The growing reliance on artificial intelligence has led to a pressing need to understand the internal workings of neural networks, particularly those used for decision-making tasks. Despite the importance of this knowledge, neural networks lack a clear causal framework, hindering efforts to analyze and modify them. This study addresses this challenge by introducing a novel concept – causal neural networks – which provides a structured framework for examining and manipulating neural networks. A key aspect of this framework is the identification of a specific condition that ensures the validity of causal interpretations. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the value of causal neural networks by applying them to tasks such as selecting relevant data and modifying network parameters. The benefits of this approach are illustrated through a classification example and an analysis of a generative adversarial network. The study also discusses the potential for integrating causal neural networks with other machine learning techniques. The underlying mathematics is explained in a companion paper titled "Causal Neural Networks: A Mathematical Foundation". The weak b-principle states that given a map f between infinite metric spaces and a collection of subspaces with specific properties, if there's an approximate representation of f through a combination of embeddings from a certain class that respect the collection, then there's an exact representation of f up to a minimal error. A particular case of the weak b-principle is then used to prove the Mumford Conjecture for a particular genus of surfaces. Additionally, another instance of the weak b-principle is utilized to establish the homeomorphism group of a specific surface is generated by homeomorphisms that can be represented by certain embeddings of subspaces. Furthermore, this leads to the discovery that the homeomorphism group of this surface has a specific property, and it is also homeomorphic to another group, thereby providing another proof for this property. Lastly, the paper also includes a discussion on the relationship between the weak b-principle and the smooth b-principle.

This issue could be resolved if the star's spin decays to 1-2 days, allowing a surface solid layer to form. This scenario is consistent with the observed rapid spin in V249A, and may be linked to the ingestion of a massive planetary object with a large angular momentum, or alternatively, to unexpected angular momentum transfer from the surrounding accretion disk. This model also suggests that the star's spin decay could be driven by magnetic coupling with the disk, leading to a longer spin decay period than previously estimated. This may have implications for the formation of solid surface layers in T Tauri stars, and the ingestion of massive planetary objects in the early stages of star formation. This model can be tested by future observations of the star's spin period and surface solid layer. The proposed framework offers a versatile tool for researchers and practitioners to gain a deeper understanding of complex systems and their dynamics. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end speech enhancement approach called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which simultaneously processes multiple channels and produces an individualized output. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the creation of more efficient implementations of the evaluation function, which can selectively apply cancellation to specific instances of equality, rather than universally cancelling all equalities. By doing so, we can maintain the consistency of the system while allowing the evaluation to proceed at a faster pace. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we provide an optimized version of the Goualard's surface proof, which features a substantial reduction in evaluation time. Furthermore, we contend that the inverse bell curve hypothesis may be an oversimplification that neglects the complexities of human relationships and group interactions. To support this perspective, we draw on examples from chess players, the civil rights movement, and the sports world, highlighting how highly intelligent individuals can contribute to a group's success by taking on supporting roles, facilitating collaboration, and driving innovation. By considering the multifaceted nature of group intelligence, we hope to encourage a more nuanced exploration of the inverse bell curve hypothesis. Recently introduced dynamic layer normalization (DLN) has shown significant
improvement in sequence transduction tasks by treating input sequences as dynamic
parameters. However, processing long sequences with DLN is computationally
expensive due to its full attention mechanism. In this paper, we propose a novel
cost-effective approach called Dynamic Entrance with Global Mean Pooling (DEGMP)
to replace DLN for short sequence applications. DEGMP leverages the global
coherence of input sequences by utilizing a global mean, and we demonstrate its
effectiveness on several short sequence tasks including speech recognition and
machine translation. Experiment results show that DEGMP achieves comparable
performance to DLN while significantly reducing the computational cost. Moreover,
DEGMP can be applied to both feed-forward and recurrent networks. Code for the
proposed method is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-hu/DEGMP.

However, the vast amount of available knowledge on the internet makes it challenging to develop an effective question knowledge retrieval approach. To address this issue, we propose a novel Coarse-to-Precise (C2P) framework that leverages semantic representations to guide the question knowledge retrieval process. The growing need for privacy in machine learning has driven the development of federated learning, where a central server trains a model using data from end devices across a network. Optimizing the model occurs locally on each device before being sent to the server, where an average of the model updates is calculated across all devices. However, this process is often hindered by communication constraints, leading researchers to explore asynchronous accumulation techniques. These methods enable the server to aggregate model updates in batches, allowing devices to send unconstrained gradients to the server. In our research, we present a novel asynchronous accumulation framework that incorporates a buffer system to manage delayed updates. This approach ensures that the server only aggregates updates from devices that have successfully completed their local training sessions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments using real-world datasets, which show that it outperforms existing techniques in terms of model accuracy and training time. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the method's convergence properties, which support our empirical findings. Our approach has been implemented in the PyTorch Federated Learning framework, and the code is available for public use.

Integrating visual and inertial sensors provides a compact and self-contained navigation system with the potential to be highly accurate, but it also poses significant challenges due to the noisy nature of inertial measurements and the occlusions that can affect visual data. To address these issues, a novel end-to-end deep learning method called EMA-VIO has been developed to efficiently navigate indoor environments using a visual-inertial sensor fusion system. The proposed network features an external memory attention mechanism that enables the selection of relevant visual features to match the inertial measurements, thereby enhancing the accuracy of visual-inertial fusion. To further improve the system's robustness, a spatial-temporal consistency loss has been incorporated to constrain the predicted poses and velocities to be consistent across different sensor modalities. Experimental evaluations conducted in various indoor environments demonstrated the superiority of EMA-VIO over existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of navigation accuracy, with an average translation error of 0.15 meters and an average rotation error of 2.45 degrees. The system's efficiency was also highlighted by its ability to operate at 20 frames per second on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. The proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub. The growing interest in conversational agents that address user emotions necessitates the development of a dataset that includes annotated data for evaluating models' ability to understand and respond to emotional content in conversations. However, creating such a dataset is challenging due to the high cost of manual annotation. This paper proposes a method to automatically annotate a specific dataset, the Emotion Related Question (ERQ) dataset, which contains 10,000 labeled question conversations. The proposed approach utilizes a pre-existing dataset with semantic annotations as a reference to guide the annotation of new, unseen data. It achieves this by training a classifier to predict the most likely annotation for a given sample based on the distribution of the reference dataset. The method is applied to the ERQ dataset, resulting in a revised version with 8,000 annotated samples. Evaluations using the original dataset show that the proposed approach is effective in revising the annotations, with a significant improvement in F1-score. Furthermore, the revised dataset demonstrates a higher correlation with human judgments of emotional content in conversations. The proposed approach and revised dataset can be utilized as a starting point for further research, including the development of models that evaluate the emotional content of conversations. This framework is then applied to solve a pressing issue in this field: determining the number of components in a mixture model. This problem is significant because it has multiple conflicting objectives, including the need for a low component count to facilitate model interpretability, versus the desire for a high component count to achieve an accurate fit to the data. To tackle this challenge, we use geometric probability to establish a non-parametric test for identifying the optimal number of components in a mixture model. This test is based on the characteristics of the model's support, which is a convex set, and it takes into account the uncertainty associated with the model. This uncertainty arises from the limited amount of data available and it affects the model's fit to the data. To account for this uncertainty, we use the theory of convex functions and Choquet capacities to develop a decision-making approach that balances the trade-offs between model interpretability and data fit. This approach is then applied to a real-world problem involving the classification of breast cancer subtypes using gene expression data. The results of this application demonstrate that the proposed approach is capable of accurately identifying the optimal number of components in a mixture model, which in turn enables the accurate classification of cancer subtypes. In recent years, neural network-based generative models have achieved significant improvements in speech synthesis quality, particularly in terms of naturalness and expressiveness. In contrast, autoregressive models have demonstrated superior performance in generating high-quality speech, yet they are computationally expensive and struggle with conditioning on complex variables like pitch. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel Quasi-Periodic WaveNet that incorporates a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network (DCNN) into an autoregressive framework. Experimental results on the LJSpeech dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a naturalness score of 4.53 and a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.42, outperforming the WaveNet and Transformer-based models in terms of naturalness and MOS.
